stops.name: Weißer Hirsch, Dresden, the sanatorium bed beside Laban's
stops.campa: Run down by the tour, she takes a cure at the Lahmann-Sanatorium on the Weißer Hirsch above Dresden, and finds, convalescing in the same corridors, a Hungarian architect turned dance-visionary named Rudolf von Laban, himself collapsed from overwork building a rival system to Dalcroze's own. The canon remembers the meeting as a thunderclap disguised as bed rest: two exhausted reformers of the body, discovering between them that music and movement need not be married at all. She leaves the sanatorium cured of her fever and infected, permanently, with his heresy.

stops.name: Munich, the break from music
stops.campa: Star pupil of Jaques-Dalcroze at Hellerau, she comes to Laban's circle in Munich and defects from eurhythmics to his camp: from movement obeying music to movement sovereign. Around them gathers the first company, musicians, painters, seekers, and Laban formulates the heresy that founds the new German dance: rhythm lives in the body before it lives in sound. Perrottet, who has spent seven years teaching bodies to count, begins learning to let hers stop counting. The Dalcroze school takes note of the apostasy of its most trusted teacher.

stops.name: Hellerau, the declaration to Nolde and Wigman
stops.campa: She returns once more to the garden city to settle her affairs with Dalcroze and finds herself, in the studio, telling the painter Emil Nolde and the still-loyal pupil Mary Wigman exactly why she is leaving: for a man on a mountain above Ascona who lets his students dance with no music at all. The sentence passes into the annals of German dance as the annunciation that sends Wigman herself to Laban within the year. Perrottet does not know, saying it, that she is handing another woman the words that will end her own oldest friendship's rivalry.
stops.quote: Und die Perrottet sagte, sie verläßt Dalcroze und geht zu einem Mann, der tolle Sachen macht, der ganz ohne Musik, seine Schüler ganz ohne Musik tanzen läßt.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman, late recollection of 1913, cited at gusto-graeser.info, 'Mary Wigman', reporting Perrottet's own words

stops.name: Vienna, the Dalcroze school she is given leave to found
stops.campa: In a last act of the old loyalty, Dalcroze grants his departing teacher his own blessing to open a school of his method in Vienna: proof that the break, however total it will become, begins as a parting in good faith rather than a scandal. She teaches the counted body one final season in the city of Freud and the Secession, drawing income and cover for what is already, privately, a different education: letters to and from Ascona, plans for a mountain she has not yet climbed.

stops.name: Monte Verità, Ascona, arrival on the sacred hill
stops.campa: She climbs the hill above Lake Maggiore where vegetarians, anarchists, sun-worshippers and theosophists have built a republic of the reformed body, and enters Laban's School for Art as his companion and first true collaborator, not his pupil. Bare feet, sun-cult robes, the prophet Gusto Gräser's grotto below the meadow: the whole colony seems built to receive exactly the apostasy she has just committed. She has spent seven years perfecting the counted step. On this hill she will spend the rest of her youth unlearning it.

stops.name: Monte Verità, Wigman climbs the hill behind her
stops.campa: Three weeks after her own arrival, Perrottet watches the sentence she spoke at Hellerau bear its fruit: Mary Wigman climbs the same path to enroll in Laban's summer course, drawn by the very words Perrottet gave Nolde. The two former Dalcroze women meet again on the mountain, no longer teacher's colleagues but co-conspirators in an art with no name. Laban now has his two strongest instruments in one meadow: the collaborator who brought him the fire, and the disciple the fire was lit to attract.

stops.name: Monte Verità, the daimon unbound, the encounter as liberating blow
stops.campa: Barefoot on the meadow, she dances for the first time to nothing but breath and gong and the swing of her own weight: the vocabulary of Ausdruckstanz smelted in real time between them. Later chroniclers of the school will call the whole encounter with Laban ein befreiender Schlag, a liberating blow, and this is its floor: tension and release, fall and recovery, music no longer required to authorize a single motion. The violinist who once notated Dalcroze's counted phrases faster than he could speak them now moves to no count at all.

stops.name: Monte Verità, the dance farm, the little kingdom
stops.campa: The second summer on the mountain: Laban's little kingdom is a working dance farm where the company gardens, cooks, weaves its own costumes and dances, art and life composted together, and Perrottet, musician, teacher, now lover and collaborator, stands at the practical center of it, keeping the school running while Laban theorizes. She and Wigman deepen the movement experiments: swings, scales, the first sketches of a harmony of space modeled on crystals. It is the last summer of the old European peace, though no one on the mountain yet knows it.

stops.name: Ascona, August 1914, the war breaks over the hill
stops.campa: The guns of Sarajevo's June echo down to the lake, and by August the frontiers close around the mountain: the international colony that made Monte Verità possible is suddenly a scatter of enemy nationals. Laban, a subject of Austria-Hungary, cannot simply cross into hostile France or Italy; the school must winter in neutral Switzerland. Perrottet, a Swiss citizen, becomes the practical passport of the whole operation: the one member of the household who can move freely across the borders now sealing around everyone she has just chosen to live with.

stops.name: Zurich, the wartime school of dance, sound and word
stops.campa: Laban moves the work to Zurich, neutral hive of exiles, spies and prophets, and opens a school of dance, sound and word with Perrottet running its daily life while he sits over graph paper hunting the alphabet of movement. She teaches, keeps the books, plays violin for classes that Dalcroze himself would no longer recognize as his method's descendant. The city fills with every avant-garde that war has washed out of Europe, and the poor, cold, incandescent studio becomes the laboratory where Ausdruckstanz is refined from mountain rite into transferable discipline.

stops.name: Hombrechtikon, the Labangarten, the triangular household
stops.campa: Beyond the city, in the orchards above the lake at Hombrechtikon, the household takes rural form: Laban, his wife Maja Lederer, their children, and Perrottet under one roof, an arrangement the canon records without scandal as a largely harmonious triangle. Here the school grows its own vegetables and its own theory at once: reform dress, handcraft, music theory, movement, taught to whoever will come. It is a commune before the word is fashionable, built on the working conviction that a dance reborn needs a life reborn to carry it.

stops.name: Hombrechtikon: Allar is born
stops.campa: On the last day of January, Perrottet bears Laban a son, Allar, later known as André Perrottet von Laban, into the same orchard household where Laban's wife's own children are already growing up. The canon does not soften the arrangement into a lesser story: Allar will inherit both names and, in time, both arts, becoming himself a dancer, choreographer and sculptor before his death in 1956. For Perrottet the birth is the deepest root her defection from Dalcroze will ever put down: flesh where the others left only technique.
